children.text: AI Meeting Notes for Schools: Why the Safest Student Data Agreement Has Almost Nothing to Cover
A FERPA-friendly AI note taker for schools. Meetily transcribes on the staff computer, with no bot, so student data never reaches us. California DPA signed.

children.alt: Sandeep Zachariah

A note from Meetily's CEO: the safest student data agreement has almost nothing to cover. Meeting notes stay on the staff computer, no bot joins the call, Meetily receives license information only, and the student data privacy agreement is signed in California

children.text: Most AI note takers used in schools send meeting data to their own servers, and that's where the FERPA questions start. Meetily keeps recordings, transcripts and summaries on the staff member's own computer by default. We've signed California's student data privacy agreement through CITE, and Meetily never receives student meeting content. Less data shared means fewer privacy concerns for schools.
There's no FERPA certification, so no AI note taker is "FERPA certified". Your district's counsel makes the final call.

In September, a data and systems analyst at a California school district sent us an 18-question review. It was one of the most thorough vendor questionnaires I've seen. Does the tool join meetings on its own? Are notes sent to every participant automatically? Is district data ever used to train AI models? Who are your subprocessors? Can it be used in a confidential IEP meeting?

These are exactly the right questions. Schools have watched AI note-takers join meetings uninvited, send summaries to everyone on the invite
(opens in new tab)
, and quietly keep recordings on servers nobody in the district chose. A parent-teacher conference, a disciplinary review or a special education meeting is not the kind of conversation anyone wants on a vendor's server.

Answering that questionnaire made something clear to me. For most AI tools, a student data privacy agreement is a long list of promises about what the vendor will do with student data. For Meetily, it is a short list, because student data never reaches us in the first place. I've come to believe that is the better standard. The safest agreement isn't the one with the strongest promises. It's the one with almost nothing to cover.
What FERPA and state student privacy laws require of AI note takers

FERPA
(opens in new tab)
 protects students' education records, and it applies to K-12 districts and to colleges and universities that receive funding from the US Department of Education. When a school lets an outside vendor access those records, the vendor typically has to act as a "school official" under the school's direct control
(opens in new tab)
, with limits on how the data can be used and shared
(opens in new tab)
.
State student privacy laws and the NDPA

States add their own layer. California's Education Code section 49073.1
(opens in new tab)
 sets out what a contract with a third party handling student records must say, and its Student Online Personal Information Protection Act
(opens in new tab)
 prohibits using student data for targeted advertising or profiling. New York
(opens in new tab)
, Illinois and many other states have similar laws. To make all of this manageable, thousands of districts now use standard agreements from the Student Data Privacy Consortium
(opens in new tab)
, such as the National Data Privacy Agreement
(opens in new tab)
 and its California version
(opens in new tab)
.

Universities face the same FERPA obligations, plus their own security reviews, often using the Higher Education Community Vendor Assessment Toolkit (HECVAT)
(opens in new tab)
, and research rules. A recorded research interview with a human subject is data an institutional review board expects to be protected
(opens in new tab)
, not uploaded to whichever note-taker a researcher happened to install.
When a meeting recording becomes an education record

Now think about what a typical AI note-taker does in a school meeting. A teacher, a counselor and a parent discuss a student's progress, behavior or disability. The tool records it and sends the audio to the vendor's servers to be transcribed and summarized. That conversation is now very likely part of an education record
(opens in new tab)
, sitting in a system the district has to vet, contract for, audit and eventually ask to delete.
How an on-device AI note taker keeps student data off vendor servers
Meetily works differently. It is a private application installed on the staff member's own Windows or Mac computer, with Linux support on the way, and it does its work there.
No bot, no calendar access, no automatic sharing

Meetily detects that a meeting has started and asks the user whether to record. Nothing starts on its own unless the user chooses to turn that on. It doesn't join the call as a bot, it doesn't read calendars, and it doesn't send anything to the other participants. Speech is transcribed on the device. Summaries are written by Meetily's built-in AI, or by any AI model the school chooses to use. Recordings, transcripts and summaries are saved on the user's own computer, or in a shared folder the school chooses. Nothing is distributed automatically. When a teacher wants to share notes, they export a normal document, and the recipient doesn't need an account to read it.

So what does Meetily actually receive? Only what we need to manage a license: the license holder's name, email address and organization, the license key, the number of seats, a device identifier used to enforce seat limits, and the app version. No audio. No transcripts. No summaries. No voiceprints. No student data. And no usage analytics from paid installations either.

children.alt: How Meetily works in a school: a staff, parent or IEP meeting starts, Meetily asks whether to record, the transcript and summary are written on the computer by default, and notes are saved on the computer or a school folder. Meetily only sees who holds the license, the organization, the license key and seats, and the device ID and app version. It never sees recordings, transcripts, summaries, voiceprints or student data, and nothing is used for AI training, advertising or resale

children.text: Everything about the meeting stays on the staff member's computer by default. The only thing Meetily ever sees is who holds the license.

That is why, when the district's questionnaire asked about subprocessors, retention and deletion, the honest answer was that there was almost nothing to describe. No subprocessor ever receives meeting content. There is no meeting data on our side to retain or delete, because it lives on the district's own devices under the district's own policies. And when it asked whether district data would ever be used to train AI models, for advertising or for resale, the answer was simple, and we put it in writing: never.

When the district asked whether we would sign a California student data privacy agreement, we said yes, and we have signed it through CITE, the California IT in Education organization
(opens in new tab)
. But the scope of that agreement tells the real story. Its schedule of data, the list of student data a vendor receives, is essentially empty, because the only information we hold is about the license holder, not about students. And because the agreement includes a General Offer of Privacy Terms, other California districts can sign on to the same terms through the Student Data Privacy Consortium instead of starting from scratch.

That changes the conversation for a district or a university. Instead of trusting a vendor to protect student records, you're choosing software that never receives them. Your counsel will always make the final determination about FERPA and state law for your own situation, and we don't claim any certification we don't hold. What we can offer is an architecture where most of the hard questions don't apply, and contract language that says so.

A thorough review deserves honest answers, including the less comfortable ones. AI transcription is very good but not perfect, and it varies with audio quality, accents and background noise. AI summaries can contain mistakes, so we recommend treating them as drafts that a person reviews before they become an official record. That matters most in the meetings schools care about most, like IEP meetings.

Consent is also a human responsibility. Because Meetily runs on the user's own computer rather than as a bot in the call, other participants don't see a notice unless the person recording tells them. We'd encourage every school to make "ask before you record" part of its meeting policy, whatever tool it uses.
Meetily Enterprise for districts and universities

And for districts and universities that want to go further, Meetily Enterprise runs entirely on the institution's own servers, with no connection to us at all. IT can install Meetily silently on staff computers, set policies once that users can't change, choose which AI model everyone uses, and manage licenses without anything being sent to us.

Schools are being asked to adopt AI faster than they can review it. Teachers want help with meeting notes. Administrators want to save time. IT and privacy teams are left saying no to tools that would genuinely help, because the data path is wrong.
It doesn't have to be a choice between AI and student privacy. When the AI runs on the school's own devices, the school keeps the benefit and the vendor never gets the data.
We started Meetily on one belief. We want to bring the power of technology to our customers, but not their data to us. In a school, that belief protects the people who matter most.

If your district, college or university is reviewing AI note-takers, I'm happy to walk your IT and privacy team through how it works and the agreement. US schools can buy online or raise a purchase order through our authorized US reseller. You can book a time with me here
(opens in new tab)
.

children.q: Is there a FERPA-compliant AI note taker?
children.a: There's no FERPA certification, so no AI note taker can honestly call itself FERPA certified. FERPA sets duties for schools, and a vendor that receives student records has to work as a school official under the school's direct control. The safest setup is a tool that never receives student data at all. Meetily transcribes on the staff member's own computer by default and only receives license information, and we've signed a California student data privacy agreement. Your district's counsel makes the final call for your situation.

children.q: Is a SOC 2 or HIPAA-compliant AI note taker automatically FERPA compliant?
children.a: No. SOC 2 and HIPAA are about how a vendor protects the data it holds. FERPA asks a different question: should the vendor hold student records at all, and under what contract. A vendor with strong security still has to act as a school official under the school's direct control, with limits on how it uses and shares the records. The simplest way to meet that duty is a tool that never receives the records. Meetily transcribes on the staff member's computer by default and only receives license information.

children.q: Can I record an IEP meeting with an AI note taker?
Is an AI meeting transcript an education record under FERPA?
Does HIPAA apply to IEP and special education meetings?
Do I need consent to record a parent-teacher conference?
What should I ask an AI note-taker vendor before using it with student data?
children.a: Ask where the audio, transcripts and summaries go, and who stores them. Ask whether the tool joins meetings on its own or reads calendars, and whether it sends notes to participants automatically. Ask whether district data is ever used to train AI models, for advertising or for resale, and get the answer in writing. Ask for the list of subprocessors that receive meeting content, how retention and deletion work, and whether the vendor will sign your state's student data privacy agreement. Then look at the agreement's schedule of data: the shorter it is, the less there is to protect.

children.q: Do I need a data privacy agreement to use an AI note taker with student data?
children.a: If the vendor will receive student data, your district will almost always want one, and many states require certain terms in the contract. California's Education Code section 49073.1 is one example. Most districts use their state's version of the National Data Privacy Agreement. Ask your district's privacy or IT team before you start: many keep a list of approved tools that already have a signed agreement. Meetily has signed the California version, and its schedule of data is almost empty because we only receive license information.

children.q: What does Meetily receive when a school buys licenses?
children.a: Only what's needed to manage the license: the license holder's name, email address and organization, the license key, the number of seats, a device ID used to enforce seat limits, and the app version. Meetily doesn't receive audio, transcripts, summaries, voiceprints or student data. By default, transcription and summaries run on the staff member's computer. If a school chooses an outside AI model for summaries, the transcript text goes to that provider under the school's own account, not to Meetily.

children.q: Does Meetily use school data to train AI models?
children.a: No. Meetily never receives meeting content, so there's nothing for us to train on. We've also put it in writing for schools: district data is never used to train AI models, for advertising or for resale.

children.q: Can other California districts sign Meetily's student data privacy agreement?
children.a: Yes. Our California agreement includes a General Offer of Privacy Terms, so another California district can sign on to the same privacy terms through the Student Data Privacy Consortium registry instead of negotiating a new agreement. It covers the privacy terms only; pricing and the service agreement are separate.

children.q: Does California's AB 1159 change anything for AI note takers?
children.a:
AB 1159, signed in September 2026, expands California's student privacy laws. It bars covered ed tech companies from using student information to train generative AI or develop AI models, and it adds a new law for colleges and universities. The K-12 changes take effect on January 1, 2027, and the higher education rules on July 1, 2027 (Venable summary
(opens in new tab)
, CalMatters
(opens in new tab)
). For a tool that sends meetings to a vendor, that's a rule the vendor has to follow. Meetily never receives meeting content, so there's no student data on our side to train on, and our California agreement already says district data is never used to train AI models.

children.q: Does COPPA apply to an AI note taker teachers use?
children.a:
COPPA covers online services that collect personal information from children under 13. Meetily is installed and used by staff on their own computers, and it doesn't collect personal information from students. The FTC's 2025 update to the COPPA Rule
(opens in new tab)
 didn't add a new school-consent rule; it kept its existing guidance for schools and ed tech.

children.q: Can I use AI transcription for IRB-approved research interviews?
How do I stop AI note-taker bots from joining district meetings?
children.a: Most districts start in the admin settings of their meeting platform, by limiting which third-party apps staff can connect and who can join meetings without being let in. Then they write down which AI tools are approved for which meetings, and give staff an approved option, so people aren't tempted to sign up for a bot on their own. A tool that runs on the staff member's computer, with no bot and no calendar access, never shows up in the meeting to begin with.

children.q: Which computers does Meetily run on?
children.a: Meetily runs on Windows and Mac. Linux users can build it from the open-source code today, and a Linux installer is in development. Meetily Enterprise can run on the institution's own servers, and IT can install the app silently on staff computers.

Frequently Asked Questions
What are the risk levels of the EU AI Act?
There are four risk levels, also called risk categories. Unacceptable risk is banned outright, for example social scoring or reading people's emotions at work. High risk is allowed with strict duties, for example AI used in hiring or to evaluate workers. Limited risk carries light transparency duties, for example telling people they're talking to a chatbot or labeling AI-generated content. Minimal risk, like a spam filter, has no new duties. An AI meeting tool that transcribes and summarizes is usually minimal or limited risk. The same tool used to score staff is high risk.
Are AI meeting note takers high-risk under the EU AI Act?
Not by itself. The AI Act looks at what a tool is used for, not at the product. Recording a call, writing a transcript and producing a summary isn't on the Act's high-risk list. It becomes high-risk when the output is used to monitor or evaluate workers, or to make decisions about their promotion, dismissal or tasks. Those uses are listed in Annex III, point 4.
Can my employer use meeting transcripts to evaluate my performance?
Under the AI Act, using AI to monitor or evaluate workers' performance and behavior is a high-risk use. From 2 December 2027, an employer doing this must follow the vendor's instructions, keep a human in charge of the decisions, and tell workers' representatives and the affected workers before using it (Article 26). The GDPR and national employment law already apply today, even to a small pilot. In Germany, for example, the works council must agree before an employer introduces technical tools that can monitor staff behavior or performance (Section 87(1) no. 6 of the Works Constitution Act).
What is required for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act?
The vendor, called the provider, has to manage risks, use good-quality data, keep technical documentation and logs, design the system for human oversight, meet accuracy and security standards, run a quality management system (the part EN 18286 covers), pass a conformity assessment and register the system. The company using it, called the deployer, has to use it as instructed, give oversight to trained people, keep the logs it produces for at least six months, inform workers before using it at work, and run a data protection impact assessment where the GDPR requires one. For workplace uses, these duties start on 2 December 2027.
Do we have to tell people an AI note taker is in the meeting?
Yes. The GDPR says people must be told when their personal data is collected and why, and a meeting recording or transcript is personal data. If the output is used for a high-risk purpose at work, such as evaluating staff, the AI Act adds its own duty from December 2027 to inform workers and their representatives first. Some countries go further. In Germany, for example, secretly recording someone's spoken words can be a criminal offense under Section 201 of the Criminal Code
(opens in new tab)
. We cover how to tell people in compliant meeting notes without a bot.
Is emotion recognition in work meetings banned under the EU AI Act?
Yes. Since 2 February 2025, Article 5 of the AI Act
(opens in new tab)
 bans AI that infers the emotions of people at work or in education from biometric data, such as their tone of voice or their face on camera. The only exceptions are medical or safety reasons. It's one of a short list of banned uses, alongside social scoring and manipulative AI. According to the Commission's guidelines, inferring emotions from written text alone, such as the words in a transcript, isn't covered by the ban (Future of Privacy Forum summary
(opens in new tab)
).
Has the EU AI Act been delayed to 2027?
Partly, and the delay is now law. The Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, moved the main rules for high-risk AI listed in Annex III, which includes workplace uses, to 2 December 2027. High-risk AI built into regulated products moves to 2 August 2028. The bans in Article 5 and the AI literacy duty weren't delayed. Both have applied since 2 February 2025.
What is EN 18286?
EN 18286 is the first harmonized standard under the EU AI Act. It sets out how providers of high-risk AI should run a quality management system, the requirement in Article 17. It was published in the Official Journal of the EU on 14 October 2026, through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. A provider that follows it is presumed to meet that part of the law. Using it's voluntary, and standards for other areas, such as risk management and cybersecurity, are still being written.
Who is responsible under the AI Act: the meeting tool vendor or the company using it?
Both, for different things. The vendor, which the Act calls the provider, answers for how the tool is built. The company using it, which the Act calls the deployer, answers for how it's used. Buying from a careful vendor doesn't cover you if you use the tool's output for a high-risk purpose, such as rating employees.
Who needs to comply with the EU AI Act?
Anyone who builds, sells or uses AI in a professional setting in the EU. That covers providers, which build the system or put it on the market, and deployers, which use it at work, plus importers and distributors. It also reaches companies outside the EU when their AI is sold in the EU or its output is used there (Article 2). So a US company with staff or customers in Europe should assume it applies. Purely personal, non-professional use is out of scope.
What does the AI literacy duty mean for teams using AI meeting tools?
Article 4 asks companies that use AI to take steps so their people understand the tools they use, including what the tools can get wrong and what they must not be used for. Since the Digital Omnibus, the duty is about making the effort, not reaching a fixed level for each person. A short internal record of the training you have done is a sensible way to show it.
Does running a meeting tool on our own devices make us compliant?
No. Where the data sits doesn't decide how the tool is used, so local processing can't make anyone compliant on its own. What it does is remove some questions. With Meetily, transcription runs on your device by default, so there is no audio transfer to another country and no vendor copy of the recording. For summaries, you pick a local model or your own API key with a provider you choose. If you use your own key, the transcript text goes to that provider under your account.
Does the GDPR still apply to AI meeting recordings?
Yes. Nothing in the AI Act replaces the GDPR. A recording of people who can be identified is personal data. So the usual questions still apply: your legal basis, such as consent, the purpose, how long you keep it, and where it's stored. Our GDPR guide for meeting transcription walks through each one.

Your Meeting Tool's Risk Level Under the EU AI Act Isn't Set by the Vendor. It's Set by You.

The EU AI Act's four risk categories cover uses, not products. The same meeting tool can be low-risk, high-risk or banned. Plus the 2027 timeline and EN 18286.

Sandeep Zachariah
CEO, Zackriya Solutions
OCTOBER 24, 2026
·
5 MIN READ
·
PRIVACY & SECURITY
·
ENGLISH

TL;DR

The EU AI Act sorts AI into four risk levels: banned, high-risk, limited and minimal. It classifies how you use AI, not just the tool itself. Transcribing and summarizing meetings isn't high-risk, but using the transcripts to score employees can be. Reading people's emotions at work has been banned since February 2025, with narrow exceptions for medical and safety reasons.

The high-risk rules for workplace uses now start on 2 December 2027, but the AI literacy duty already applies. EN 18286, the first harmonized standard under the Act, came out on 14 October 2026. And the GDPR still covers your meeting recordings (our GDPR guide for meeting transcription). Keeping meetings on your own device makes some questions simpler, like transfers abroad, but it doesn't make you compliant on its own.

The key takeaway: your vendor is responsible for how the tool is built. You're responsible for how you use it.

On 14 October, the European Union cited its first harmonized standard under the AI Act
(opens in new tab)
. It's called EN 18286, and it describes how providers of high-risk AI should run their quality management. If a provider builds its system on it, regulators will presume that part of the law is met.

Most people using AI in their meetings will never open this standard, and most don't need to. It covers one of ten areas the Commission asked for, and the rest are still being written. But I think it matters for a different reason. It is the moment the AI Act
(opens in new tab)
 stopped being something people discuss and started becoming something people build against. And when that happens, the question every organization will eventually be asked is a simple one: what AI are you using, and what are you using it for?

For AI meeting tools, I don't think most organizations can answer that yet.

Here is what I've come to believe after a lot of conversations with European teams. The AI Act does not really classify products. It classifies uses. The same piece of software can sit in very different places depending on what you do with it, and the person who decides that is usually not the vendor. It's you.

Take a meeting assistant that transcribes a project call and writes a summary. For most purposes, that is a low-risk use. Now take the same transcript and feed it into a process that scores how employees perform in meetings, or decides who gets flagged for review. The Act lists AI used to monitor and evaluate workers' performance and behavior as high-risk
(opens in new tab)
. Same tool, same audio, very different obligations. And if a tool tries to infer the emotions of people at work, from their tone of voice or their face on camera, that use has been prohibited in the EU since February 2025
(opens in new tab)
, apart from narrow medical and safety cases.

HOW YOU USE THE MEETING TOOL	RISK LEVEL UNDER THE EU AI ACT	WHEN THE RULES APPLY
Transcribe a project call and create a summary	Generally not high-risk (minimal or limited risk). The GDPR still applies to recordings and transcripts.	GDPR applies now
Use meeting transcripts to rate employee performance	High-risk: AI used to monitor and evaluate workers.	2 December 2027

Frequently Asked Questions
What are the risk levels of the EU AI Act?
There are four risk levels, also called risk categories. Unacceptable risk is banned outright, for example social scoring or reading people's emotions at work. High risk is allowed with strict duties, for example AI used in hiring or to evaluate workers. Limited risk carries light transparency duties, for example telling people they're talking to a chatbot or labeling AI-generated content. Minimal risk, like a spam filter, has no new duties. An AI meeting tool that transcribes and summarizes is usually minimal or limited risk. The same tool used to score staff is high risk.
Are AI meeting note takers high-risk under the EU AI Act?
Not by itself. The AI Act looks at what a tool is used for, not at the product. Recording a call, writing a transcript and producing a summary isn't on the Act's high-risk list. It becomes high-risk when the output is used to monitor or evaluate workers, or to make decisions about their promotion, dismissal or tasks. Those uses are listed in Annex III, point 4.
Can my employer use meeting transcripts to evaluate my performance?
Under the AI Act, using AI to monitor or evaluate workers' performance and behavior is a high-risk use. From 2 December 2027, an employer doing this must follow the vendor's instructions, keep a human in charge of the decisions, and tell workers' representatives and the affected workers before using it (Article 26). The GDPR and national employment law already apply today, even to a small pilot. In Germany, for example, the works council must agree before an employer introduces technical tools that can monitor staff behavior or performance (Section 87(1) no. 6 of the Works Constitution Act).
What is required for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act?
The vendor, called the provider, has to manage risks, use good-quality data, keep technical documentation and logs, design the system for human oversight, meet accuracy and security standards, run a quality management system (the part EN 18286 covers), pass a conformity assessment and register the system. The company using it, called the deployer, has to use it as instructed, give oversight to trained people, keep the logs it produces for at least six months, inform workers before using it at work, and run a data protection impact assessment where the GDPR requires one. For workplace uses, these duties start on 2 December 2027.
Do we have to tell people an AI note taker is in the meeting?
Yes. The GDPR says people must be told when their personal data is collected and why, and a meeting recording or transcript is personal data. If the output is used for a high-risk purpose at work, such as evaluating staff, the AI Act adds its own duty from December 2027 to inform workers and their representatives first. Some countries go further. In Germany, for example, secretly recording someone's spoken words can be a criminal offense under Section 201 of the Criminal Code
(opens in new tab)
. We cover how to tell people in compliant meeting notes without a bot.
Is emotion recognition in work meetings banned under the EU AI Act?
Yes. Since 2 February 2025, Article 5 of the AI Act
(opens in new tab)
 bans AI that infers the emotions of people at work or in education from biometric data, such as their tone of voice or their face on camera. The only exceptions are medical or safety reasons. It's one of a short list of banned uses, alongside social scoring and manipulative AI. According to the Commission's guidelines, inferring emotions from written text alone, such as the words in a transcript, isn't covered by the ban (Future of Privacy Forum summary
(opens in new tab)
).
Has the EU AI Act been delayed to 2027?
Partly, and the delay is now law. The Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, moved the main rules for high-risk AI listed in Annex III, which includes workplace uses, to 2 December 2027. High-risk AI built into regulated products moves to 2 August 2028. The bans in Article 5 and the AI literacy duty weren't delayed. Both have applied since 2 February 2025.
What is EN 18286?
EN 18286 is the first harmonized standard under the EU AI Act. It sets out how providers of high-risk AI should run a quality management system, the requirement in Article 17. It was published in the Official Journal of the EU on 14 October 2026, through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. A provider that follows it is presumed to meet that part of the law. Using it's voluntary, and standards for other areas, such as risk management and cybersecurity, are still being written.
Who is responsible under the AI Act: the meeting tool vendor or the company using it?
Both, for different things. The vendor, which the Act calls the provider, answers for how the tool is built. The company using it, which the Act calls the deployer, answers for how it's used. Buying from a careful vendor doesn't cover you if you use the tool's output for a high-risk purpose, such as rating employees.
Who needs to comply with the EU AI Act?
Anyone who builds, sells or uses AI in a professional setting in the EU. That covers providers, which build the system or put it on the market, and deployers, which use it at work, plus importers and distributors. It also reaches companies outside the EU when their AI is sold in the EU or its output is used there (Article 2). So a US company with staff or customers in Europe should assume it applies. Purely personal, non-professional use is out of scope.
What does the AI literacy duty mean for teams using AI meeting tools?
Article 4 asks companies that use AI to take steps so their people understand the tools they use, including what the tools can get wrong and what they must not be used for. Since the Digital Omnibus, the duty is about making the effort, not reaching a fixed level for each person. A short internal record of the training you have done is a sensible way to show it.
Does running a meeting tool on our own devices make us compliant?
No. Where the data sits doesn't decide how the tool is used, so local processing can't make anyone compliant on its own. What it does is remove some questions. With Meetily, transcription runs on your device by default, so there is no audio transfer to another country and no vendor copy of the recording. For summaries, you pick a local model or your own API key with a provider you choose. If you use your own key, the transcript text goes to that provider under your account.
Does the GDPR still apply to AI meeting recordings?
Yes. Nothing in the AI Act replaces the GDPR. A recording of people who can be identified is personal data. So the usual questions still apply: your legal basis, such as consent, the purpose, how long you keep it, and where it's stored. Our GDPR guide for meeting transcription walks through each one.

Frequently asked questions
Can I record or transcribe a Teams meeting if I'm not the host or organizer?
Yes, if you're in the organizer's company, your account has permission, and the meeting options let you. Guests and people from other companies can't. If the options are locked, ask the organizer to record or share the transcript. Or record on your own computer, if everyone agrees and your company allows it.
Can I record or transcribe a Teams meeting just for myself?
A Teams recording is saved to the organizer's OneDrive (or the channel's SharePoint site), and people in the organizer's company can view it. If you want a private record that isn't a shared Teams transcript, a desktop recorder saves the file on your own laptop. You still need to tell the others in the call.
Is there a way to transcribe a Teams meeting without everyone knowing?
An app on your own computer doesn't show anything in Teams. That doesn't make it OK to record people without telling them. In many places it's against the law, and it breaks most company policies. Tell everyone and get their agreement first. Meetily reminds you to do this every time you start a recording.
Will Teams or my IT team know if I use a recording app?
Teams doesn't post anything in the meeting when a separate app records your computer's audio. But your company's device-management tools may see which apps are installed or running. Don't count on going unnoticed. Follow your company's policy.
Is it legal to record a Teams meeting?
It depends on where you and the other people are. Some places need everyone's consent, and others need only one person's. The safe habit is to tell everyone and record only if they agree. This isn't legal advice, so check the laws that apply to you and your company's policy.
Can I record or transcribe a Teams meeting for free?
Yes. If your work or school plan lets you record, recording and transcription are included, and you don't need Copilot or Teams Premium. On Teams Free, recording needs a paid Microsoft 365 plan, and Microsoft documents live captions but not saved transcripts. Meetily Community is a free, open-source app that records and transcribes Teams calls on your own computer.
What's the difference between recording and transcription in Teams?
A recording is a video or audio file. A transcript is the text of what people said, with their names and timestamps. You can have both, or run a transcript on its own.
Can Teams record and transcribe automatically?
Yes, if your admin allows it. The organizer turns on Record and transcribe automatically in the meeting options for each meeting. It's off by default. See Microsoft's page on automatic recording
(opens in new tab)
.

How to Record and Transcribe a Teams Meeting Without a Bot
How to Record and Transcribe a Teams Meeting Without a Bot

Record and transcribe a Teams meeting with Teams itself, or on your laptop with a free, open-source app. No bot joins. Tell people first.

Meetily Team
Zackriya Solutions
OCTOBER 22, 2026
·
11 MIN READ
·
GUIDES
·
ENGLISH

Microsoft Teams can record and transcribe meetings if your account and the meeting settings allow it. If those options aren't available to you, an app on your own computer can do it instead. It records the audio and makes a transcript without joining the meeting as a bot.

Whichever way you go, tell everyone in the meeting before you start.

TL;DR

Short answer: In Teams, open More → Record and transcribe and choose Start recording or Start transcription. If you're a guest, or recording is turned off for you, those options are locked. A desktop app such as Meetily Community, which is free and open source, can record the audio playing on your computer and transcribe it right there, with no bot in the call.

Meetily Community is free and open source. It runs on Windows and Mac, transcribes on your own computer, and never joins the call as a bot. Download Meetily.

A sample Teams call on the right and Meetily's live transcript on the left, with no bot in the meeting

Can Microsoft Teams record and transcribe a meeting on its own?

Yes. Teams has its own tools for recording meetings and making transcripts. Whether you can use them depends on your account, your permissions and the organizer's company settings.

A recording is a video or audio file. A transcript is the words people said, with their names and timestamps. When you start a recording, Teams starts the transcript too, as long as transcription is allowed. You can also start a transcript without recording.

How do I start recording or transcription in Teams?

Do this during the meeting. It takes three steps.

Step 1: Select More (the three dots)

Select More (the three dots) in the meeting controls.

Step 2: Open Record and transcribe

Open Record and transcribe to see the recording options.

Teams meeting menu: More, then Record and transcribe, showing Start recording and Start transcription

Step 3: Choose Start recording or Start transcription

Choose Start recording for a recording and a transcript. Choose Start transcription for a transcript only. In the version we tested, Start transcription made a text transcript without a video file.

If you choose Start recording, Teams asks which language people are speaking and what to record: video and audio, or audio only. Then it starts the recording and the transcript.

Teams dialog titled Start recording and transcription, with spoken language and what to record

Your menu may look a little different, because Microsoft moves things around between versions. Microsoft's guide to recording a meeting
(opens in new tab)
 has the current steps.

Do I need Copilot or Teams Premium to transcribe a meeting?

No. Transcription is a standard Teams feature, and it's turned on by default. You don't need Copilot or Teams Premium just to get a transcript. Your company can still turn it off. See Microsoft's page on transcription and captions
(opens in new tab)
.

Teams transcription is AI speech-to-text, and the transcript panel says so: "AI-generated content may be incorrect." Copilot and Teams Premium add an intelligent recap
(opens in new tab)
 on top, with AI notes, tasks and mentions.

If your company turns transcription off, your recordings won't come with a transcript.

Where is my Teams recording saved, and how long is it kept?

For a regular meeting, Teams saves the recording to the organizer's OneDrive. For a channel meeting, it goes to the channel's SharePoint site. See Microsoft's page on meeting recordings
(opens in new tab)
.

Recordings expire after 120 days by default, and admins can change that. In the company account we tested, Teams showed 60 days. Read about recording expiration
(opens in new tab)
.

Teams meeting chat saying the recording has been saved to OneDrive and will expire in 60 days

How do I download a Teams transcript?
Open the meeting chat.
Go to Recap.
Find Transcript and select Download.
Choose .docx (a Word file) or .vtt (a subtitle file).

By default, only the organizer and co-organizers can download it. If you need a copy, ask the organizer to share it or to make you a co-organizer.

Teams Recap transcript panel with Download as .docx and Download as .vtt

Can you transcribe a Teams meeting without recording it?

Yes. Pick the option that matches what you need:

Start transcription only. Teams saves a transcript but no video.
Use Copilot "only during the meeting". You can ask Copilot questions during the call, and no transcript is kept afterward. It needs a Copilot license, and your admin has to allow it.
Turn on live captions. Words appear on screen as people talk, but nothing is saved.
Record on your own computer. A desktop app captures the call audio and turns it into text on your computer.
Start transcription only

Select More → Record and transcribe → Start transcription. Teams saves the transcript in the meeting's Recap, but it doesn't make a video file. Everyone in the meeting is told that transcription has started.

Use Copilot "only during the meeting"

If your company has Copilot and your admin allows it, the organizer can open Meeting options → Copilot and other AI and choose Only during the meeting. You can ask Copilot about the call while it's happening, but no transcript is kept afterward. See Microsoft's page on Copilot in Teams meetings
(opens in new tab)
.

Turn on live captions

Live captions show the spoken words on your screen. Anyone in the meeting can turn them on for themselves from the More menu. They make a call easier to follow, but you can't read them later, because Teams doesn't save them. See Microsoft's page on live captions
(opens in new tab)
.

Record on your own computer instead

A desktop app can record the sound playing on your computer, plus your microphone, and turn it into text. It doesn't join the meeting, so there's no bot in the participant list. This helps when Teams' own options are locked for you. Here's the step-by-step guide.

Why won't Teams let me record or transcribe?

Usually it's one of these:

You're a guest, or you're joining from another company.
The organizer or your IT team turned recording or transcription off.
You're on the free version of Teams.
Copilot is turned off for that meeting. When an organizer turns Copilot off, recording and transcription go off too.
It's a one-to-one Teams call, not a meeting. Calls follow a separate admin setting, and recording and transcription are off there by default.
Your meeting-notes bot is blocked or stuck in the lobby.

To see the exact reason, hover over the lock icon on Start recording. Your account needs permission, and the organizer's company decides what's allowed. See Microsoft's help page for recording problems
(opens in new tab)
.

Recording is grayed out because I'm a guest or from another company

This is the most common reason. When you join a meeting run by another company, Teams locks Start recording and Start transcription for you. The message says: "Unavailable to people in a different org from the organizer."

You can't change this from your side. Ask the organizer to record the meeting, or to share the transcript afterward.

Teams menu with Start recording and Start transcription locked: Unavailable to people in a different org from the organizer

My organizer or IT team turned it off

Admins can turn recording or transcription off for everyone, or only for some people. Organizers can also limit recording to themselves and presenters, so an attendee may be locked out even inside their own company. If the options are missing or gray in your own company's meetings, ask the organizer or your IT team.

One-to-one Teams calls work differently from meetings. They follow the calling policy, where recording and transcription are both off by default, so an admin has to turn them on. See Microsoft's list of Teams settings
(opens in new tab)
.

If your company turned recording off on purpose, don't try to get around it. Check the policy before you use another app.

I'm on the free version of Teams

Teams Free, for personal accounts, works differently. Microsoft says you need a paid Microsoft 365 Personal, Family or Premium plan to record meetings. Its help pages cover live captions for Teams Free, but not saved transcripts. See recordings in Teams Free
(opens in new tab)
.

My meeting-notes bot is stuck in the lobby or blocked

Many meeting assistants join the call as a bot. By default, Teams keeps bots it recognizes in the lobby until someone lets them in. See managing external bots
(opens in new tab)
.

Microsoft is also rolling out an admin setting in October 2026 that blocks these bots completely. It stays off unless an admin turns it on. See the Message center notice MC1459141
(opens in new tab)
 (an unofficial mirror of Microsoft's admin notices).

An app that records on your own computer doesn't join the meeting, so it never waits in the lobby.

Step-by-step: Recording and transcribing locally without a bot

Use a desktop app that records your computer's audio and transcribes it on the same computer. This guide uses Meetily Community.

You need a Mac with Apple Silicon, or a Windows PC with an x64 processor that supports AVX2.

Step 1: Tell everyone you're recording

Before you start, tell the people in the meeting. You could say:

"I'm recording the audio on my laptop so I can take notes."

Say it at the start of the call, or post it in the meeting chat. Teams won't announce it, so this part is up to you. Check your company's recording policy too.

Step 2: Install Meetily Community (free and open source)

Download Meetily from meetily.ai/downloads and install it like any other app. You don't need an account.

The install guide has screenshots for Windows and Mac. The code is on GitHub
(opens in new tab)
.

Step 3: Allow microphone and system audio access

Meetily needs two things:

Your microphone, to hear you.
System audio, to hear everyone else in the Teams call.

Allow both when the app asks.

On a Mac, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording. Under System Audio Recording Only, turn on meetily.

macOS System Settings, System Audio Recording Only, with meetily turned on

Step 4: Wait for the models to download

The first time you open Meetily, it downloads a speech-to-text model of about 670 MB, then a summary model. This takes a few minutes, once.

After that, transcription runs on your computer, with nothing more to download.

Step 5: Start recording, then join the Teams call

Select the red microphone button to start recording. Then join the Teams meeting in the desktop app or your browser. That way you don't miss the start of the call.

Meetily ready to record, with the red record button

Each time you start recording, Meetily reminds you to tell everyone. Once you have, select I've Notified Participants.

Meetily reminder: Recording Started. Inform all participants this meeting is being recorded.

The words show up in the transcript as people speak. Meetily isn't in the call, so nothing changes in the Teams participant list.

Step 6: Read the transcript and make a summary

When the meeting ends, stop the recording and select Generate Summary. Meetily writes a summary with key decisions, action items and discussion highlights.

Under AI Model, you choose what writes the summary: the built-in local model, a model on your computer through Ollama, or your own API key for a provider such as OpenAI or Anthropic.

Meetily Model Settings with Ollama selected as the summarization model

Meetily showing a sample Teams call transcript on the left and the generated summary on the right

Step 7: Copy your notes

Select Copy above the transcript or the summary. Then paste it into your notes, an email or your task tracker. The summary keeps its formatting.

If only one side is recorded, or you hear an echo
Only the other people are recorded: Meetily is missing microphone access, or it's listening to the wrong microphone. On a Mac, check System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone. If you use a headset, pick its microphone in Settings → Recording.
Only your voice is recorded: system audio access is missing. See Step 3.
Echo or doubled voices: wear headphones, so your microphone doesn't pick up your speakers.
Bluetooth headset on a Mac: update Meetily to the latest version. Version 0.4.1 fixed a Bluetooth microphone issue.
Wrong microphone or speakers: pick the right ones in Settings → Recording.
Will participants know if I record or transcribe a Teams meeting?

If Teams records or transcribes, Teams tells everyone in the meeting. If you record on your own computer, Teams shows nothing, because no bot joins and Teams didn't start the recording.

So you need to tell people yourself. Meetily reminds you each time you start.

What participants see when Teams records

Teams shows a notice when recording or transcription starts, and the meeting chat notes who started and stopped it. Here's what the person who started it sees:

Teams notice: Recording and transcription. Started by you. Let everyone know they're being included.

Admins can also turn on a setting that asks people to agree before they're recorded. It's off by default. See Microsoft's page on participant agreement
(opens in new tab)
.

What happens when I record on my own computer?

Nothing appears in the Teams meeting. There's no new participant, banner or chat message. The recording stays on your computer.

When should I ask first, or stop recording?

Follow your company's rules and the laws where the people in the meeting are. Ask first if the meeting covers HR, legal, health or customer matters, or if people from outside your company are on the call. Stop if someone objects.

What is the best way to record a Teams meeting?

If you're allowed to record in Teams, that's usually the simplest way. If you can't, recording on your own computer is a good fallback, as long as the people in the meeting agree and your company allows it.

	TEAMS RECORDING OR TRANSCRIPTION	COPILOT "ONLY DURING THE MEETING"	MEETING-NOTES BOT	RECORD ON YOUR OWN COMPUTER (MEETILY)
Joins the meeting as a participant	No	No	Yes	No
Does Teams tell everyone?	Yes	Microsoft doesn't say	The bot shows in the participant list	No, you tell them
Where is it saved?	Organizer's OneDrive (channel meetings: SharePoint)	No transcript saved	Usually the bot company's servers	Your computer
Where is the audio turned into text?	Microsoft	Microsoft	The bot company	Your computer, by default
What do you need?	License and permission for you and the organizer	A Copilot license	Someone to let the bot in	A Mac with Apple Silicon or a Windows PC
Cost	Included with eligible plans	Paid add-on	Varies	Community edition is free

Which one fits:

You're allowed to record in Teams: use Teams' own tools.
You want help during the call but no saved transcript, and you have Copilot: use "only during the meeting".
You're a guest, or recording is locked for you: ask the organizer to record or share the transcript. If everyone agrees and your company allows it, record on your own computer.
Your IT team blocks meeting bots: a desktop recorder works, because it doesn't join the call.
Your company turned recording off on purpose: ask IT first. Don't assume another app is allowed.
What should IT teams know about recording on your own device?

A desktop recorder such as Meetily doesn't join meetings as a bot. It doesn't need calendar access, and it doesn't send anything to the people in the meeting. It records the computer's audio, and transcription runs on that computer by default.

For summaries, people can use a local model or add their own API key. With an outside AI provider, the transcript text goes to that provider to make the summary.

So meeting audio doesn't have to go to a meeting-notes company. But it's still a recording, so your recording policy, consent rules and data-retention rules apply. IT teams that block meeting bots often want a clear rule for desktop recorders too. For more, see compliant meeting notes without a bot.

It depends on where you and the other people are. Some places need everyone's consent, and others need only one person's. The safe habit is to tell everyone and record only if they agree. This isn't legal advice, so check the laws that apply to you and your company's policy.

children.text: Microsoft Teams can record and transcribe meetings if your account and the meeting settings allow it. If those options aren't available to you, an app on your own computer can do it instead. It records the audio and makes a transcript without joining the meeting as a bot.
Whichever way you go, tell everyone in the meeting before you start.

Short answer: In Teams, open More → Record and transcribe and choose Start recording or Start transcription. If you're a guest, or recording is turned off for you, those options are locked. A desktop app such as Meetily Community, which is free and open source, can record the audio playing on your computer and transcribe it right there, with no bot in the call.
Meetily Community is free and open source. It runs on Windows and Mac, transcribes on your own computer, and never joins the call as a bot. Download Meetily.
A sample Teams call on the right and Meetily's live transcript on the left, with no bot in the meeting
Can Microsoft Teams record and transcribe a meeting on its own?
Yes. Teams has its own tools for recording meetings and making transcripts. Whether you can use them depends on your account, your permissions and the organizer's company settings.

A recording is a video or audio file. A transcript is the words people said, with their names and timestamps. When you start a recording, Teams starts the transcript too, as long as transcription is allowed. You can also start a transcript without recording.
How do I start recording or transcription in Teams?
Do this during the meeting. It takes three steps.
Select More (the three dots) in the meeting controls.
Open Record and transcribe to see the recording options.
Teams meeting menu: More, then Record and transcribe, showing Start recording and Start transcription
Step 3: Choose Start recording or Start transcription
Choose Start recording for a recording and a transcript. Choose Start transcription for a transcript only. In the version we tested, Start transcription made a text transcript without a video file.
If you choose Start recording, Teams asks which language people are speaking and what to record: video and audio, or audio only. Then it starts the recording and the transcript.
Teams dialog titled Start recording and transcription, with spoken language and what to record

Your menu may look a little different, because Microsoft moves things around between versions. Microsoft's guide to recording a meeting
(opens in new tab)
 has the current steps.
Do I need Copilot or Teams Premium to transcribe a meeting?

No. Transcription is a standard Teams feature, and it's turned on by default. You don't need Copilot or Teams Premium just to get a transcript. Your company can still turn it off. See Microsoft's page on transcription and captions
(opens in new tab)
.

Teams transcription is AI speech-to-text, and the transcript panel says so: "AI-generated content may be incorrect." Copilot and Teams Premium add an intelligent recap
(opens in new tab)
 on top, with AI notes, tasks and mentions.
If your company turns transcription off, your recordings won't come with a transcript.
Where is my Teams recording saved, and how long is it kept?

For a regular meeting, Teams saves the recording to the organizer's OneDrive. For a channel meeting, it goes to the channel's SharePoint site. See Microsoft's page on meeting recordings
(opens in new tab)
.

Recordings expire after 120 days by default, and admins can change that. In the company account we tested, Teams showed 60 days. Read about recording expiration
(opens in new tab)
.
Teams meeting chat saying the recording has been saved to OneDrive and will expire in 60 days
How do I download a Teams transcript?
Choose .docx (a Word file) or .vtt (a subtitle file).
By default, only the organizer and co-organizers can download it. If you need a copy, ask the organizer to share it or to make you a co-organizer.
Teams Recap transcript panel with Download as .docx and Download as .vtt
Can you transcribe a Teams meeting without recording it?
Yes. Pick the option that matches what you need:
Start transcription only. Teams saves a transcript but no video.
Use Copilot "only during the meeting". You can ask Copilot questions during the call, and no transcript is kept afterward. It needs a Copilot license, and your admin has to allow it.
Turn on live captions. Words appear on screen as people talk, but nothing is saved.
Record on your own computer. A desktop app captures the call audio and turns it into text on your computer.

Select More → Record and transcribe → Start transcription. Teams saves the transcript in the meeting's Recap, but it doesn't make a video file. Everyone in the meeting is told that transcription has started.

If your company has Copilot and your admin allows it, the organizer can open Meeting options → Copilot and other AI and choose Only during the meeting. You can ask Copilot about the call while it's happening, but no transcript is kept afterward. See Microsoft's page on Copilot in Teams meetings
(opens in new tab)
.

Live captions show the spoken words on your screen. Anyone in the meeting can turn them on for themselves from the More menu. They make a call easier to follow, but you can't read them later, because Teams doesn't save them. See Microsoft's page on live captions
(opens in new tab)
.
Record on your own computer instead

A desktop app can record the sound playing on your computer, plus your microphone, and turn it into text. It doesn't join the meeting, so there's no bot in the participant list. This helps when Teams' own options are locked for you. Here's the step-by-step guide.
Why won't Teams let me record or transcribe?
You're a guest, or you're joining from another company.
The organizer or your IT team turned recording or transcription off.
You're on the free version of Teams.
Copilot is turned off for that meeting. When an organizer turns Copilot off, recording and transcription go off too.
It's a one-to-one Teams call, not a meeting. Calls follow a separate admin setting, and recording and transcription are off there by default.
Your meeting-notes bot is blocked or stuck in the lobby.

To see the exact reason, hover over the lock icon on Start recording. Your account needs permission, and the organizer's company decides what's allowed. See Microsoft's help page for recording problems
(opens in new tab)
.
Recording is grayed out because I'm a guest or from another company

This is the most common reason. When you join a meeting run by another company, Teams locks Start recording and Start transcription for you. The message says: "Unavailable to people in a different org from the organizer."
You can't change this from your side. Ask the organizer to record the meeting, or to share the transcript afterward.
Teams menu with Start recording and Start transcription locked: Unavailable to people in a different org from the organizer
My organizer or IT team turned it off

Admins can turn recording or transcription off for everyone, or only for some people. Organizers can also limit recording to themselves and presenters, so an attendee may be locked out even inside their own company. If the options are missing or gray in your own company's meetings, ask the organizer or your IT team.

One-to-one Teams calls work differently from meetings. They follow the calling policy, where recording and transcription are both off by default, so an admin has to turn them on. See Microsoft's list of Teams settings
(opens in new tab)
.
If your company turned recording off on purpose, don't try to get around it. Check the policy before you use another app.
I'm on the free version of Teams

Teams Free, for personal accounts, works differently. Microsoft says you need a paid Microsoft 365 Personal, Family or Premium plan to record meetings. Its help pages cover live captions for Teams Free, but not saved transcripts. See recordings in Teams Free
(opens in new tab)
.
My meeting-notes bot is stuck in the lobby or blocked

Many meeting assistants join the call as a bot. By default, Teams keeps bots it recognizes in the lobby until someone lets them in. See managing external bots
(opens in new tab)
.

Microsoft is also rolling out an admin setting in October 2026 that blocks these bots completely. It stays off unless an admin turns it on. See the Message center notice MC1459141
(opens in new tab)
 (an unofficial mirror of Microsoft's admin notices).
An app that records on your own computer doesn't join the meeting, so it never waits in the lobby.
Step-by-step: Recording and transcribing locally without a bot
Use a desktop app that records your computer's audio and transcribes it on the same computer. This guide uses Meetily Community.
You need a Mac with Apple Silicon, or a Windows PC with an x64 processor that supports AVX2.
Before you start, tell the people in the meeting. You could say:
"I'm recording the audio on my laptop so I can take notes."
Say it at the start of the call, or post it in the meeting chat. Teams won't announce it, so this part is up to you. Check your company's recording policy too.
Step 2: Install Meetily Community (free and open source)
Download Meetily from meetily.ai/downloads and install it like any other app. You don't need an account.

The install guide has screenshots for Windows and Mac. The code is on GitHub
(opens in new tab)
.
Step 3: Allow microphone and system audio access
System audio, to hear everyone else in the Teams call.
Allow both when the app asks.
On a Mac, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording. Under System Audio Recording Only, turn on meetily.
macOS System Settings, System Audio Recording Only, with meetily turned on
Step 4: Wait for the models to download
The first time you open Meetily, it downloads a speech-to-text model of about 670 MB, then a summary model. This takes a few minutes, once.
After that, transcription runs on your computer, with nothing more to download.
Step 5: Start recording, then join the Teams call
Select the red microphone button to start recording. Then join the Teams meeting in the desktop app or your browser. That way you don't miss the start of the call.
Meetily ready to record, with the red record button
Each time you start recording, Meetily reminds you to tell everyone. Once you have, select I've Notified Participants.
Meetily reminder: Recording Started. Inform all participants this meeting is being recorded.
The words show up in the transcript as people speak. Meetily isn't in the call, so nothing changes in the Teams participant list.
Step 6: Read the transcript and make a summary
When the meeting ends, stop the recording and select Generate Summary. Meetily writes a summary with key decisions, action items and discussion highlights.
Under AI Model, you choose what writes the summary: the built-in local model, a model on your computer through Ollama, or your own API key for a provider such as OpenAI or Anthropic.
Meetily Model Settings with Ollama selected as the summarization model
Meetily showing a sample Teams call transcript on the left and the generated summary on the right
Select Copy above the transcript or the summary. Then paste it into your notes, an email or your task tracker. The summary keeps its formatting.
If only one side is recorded, or you hear an echo

Only the other people are recorded: Meetily is missing microphone access, or it's listening to the wrong microphone. On a Mac, check System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone. If you use a headset, pick its microphone in Settings → Recording.
Only your voice is recorded: system audio access is missing. See Step 3.
Echo or doubled voices: wear headphones, so your microphone doesn't pick up your speakers.
Bluetooth headset on a Mac: update Meetily to the latest version. Version 0.4.1 fixed a Bluetooth microphone issue.
Wrong microphone or speakers: pick the right ones in Settings → Recording.
Will participants know if I record or transcribe a Teams meeting?
If Teams records or transcribes, Teams tells everyone in the meeting. If you record on your own computer, Teams shows nothing, because no bot joins and Teams didn't start the recording.
So you need to tell people yourself. Meetily reminds you each time you start.
What participants see when Teams records
Teams shows a notice when recording or transcription starts, and the meeting chat notes who started and stopped it. Here's what the person who started it sees:
Teams notice: Recording and transcription. Started by you. Let everyone know they're being included.

Admins can also turn on a setting that asks people to agree before they're recorded. It's off by default. See Microsoft's page on participant agreement
(opens in new tab)
.
What happens when I record on my own computer?
Nothing appears in the Teams meeting. There's no new participant, banner or chat message. The recording stays on your computer.
When should I ask first, or stop recording?

Follow your company's rules and the laws where the people in the meeting are. Ask first if the meeting covers HR, legal, health or customer matters, or if people from outside your company are on the call. Stop if someone objects.
What is the best way to record a Teams meeting?

If you're allowed to record in Teams, that's usually the simplest way. If you can't, recording on your own computer is a good fallback, as long as the people in the meeting agree and your company allows it.

What should IT teams know about recording on your own device?

A desktop recorder such as Meetily doesn't join meetings as a bot. It doesn't need calendar access, and it doesn't send anything to the people in the meeting. It records the computer's audio, and transcription runs on that computer by default.
For summaries, people can use a local model or add their own API key. With an outside AI provider, the transcript text goes to that provider to make the summary.

So meeting audio doesn't have to go to a meeting-notes company. But it's still a recording, so your recording policy, consent rules and data-retention rules apply. IT teams that block meeting bots often want a clear rule for desktop recorders too. For more, see compliant meeting notes without a bot.

children.q: Can I record or transcribe a Teams meeting if I'm not the host or organizer?
children.a: Yes, if you're in the organizer's company, your account has permission, and the meeting options let you. Guests and people from other companies can't. If the options are locked, ask the organizer to record or share the transcript. Or record on your own computer, if everyone agrees and your company allows it.

children.q: Can I record or transcribe a Teams meeting just for myself?
children.a: A Teams recording is saved to the organizer's OneDrive (or the channel's SharePoint site), and people in the organizer's company can view it. If you want a private record that isn't a shared Teams transcript, a desktop recorder saves the file on your own laptop. You still need to tell the others in the call.

children.q: Is there a way to transcribe a Teams meeting without everyone knowing?
children.a: An app on your own computer doesn't show anything in Teams. That doesn't make it OK to record people without telling them. In many places it's against the law, and it breaks most company policies. Tell everyone and get their agreement first. Meetily reminds you to do this every time you start a recording.

children.q: Will Teams or my IT team know if I use a recording app?
children.a: Teams doesn't post anything in the meeting when a separate app records your computer's audio. But your company's device-management tools may see which apps are installed or running. Don't count on going unnoticed. Follow your company's policy.

children.q: Is it legal to record a Teams meeting?
children.a: It depends on where you and the other people are. Some places need everyone's consent, and others need only one person's. The safe habit is to tell everyone and record only if they agree. This isn't legal advice, so check the laws that apply to you and your company's policy.

children.q: Can I record or transcribe a Teams meeting for free?
children.a: Yes. If your work or school plan lets you record, recording and transcription are included, and you don't need Copilot or Teams Premium. On Teams Free, recording needs a paid Microsoft 365 plan, and Microsoft documents live captions but not saved transcripts. Meetily Community is a free, open-source app that records and transcribes Teams calls on your own computer.

children.q: What's the difference between recording and transcription in Teams?
children.a: A recording is a video or audio file. A transcript is the text of what people said, with their names and timestamps. You can have both, or run a transcript on its own.

children.q: Can Teams record and transcribe automatically?
children.a:
Yes, if your admin allows it. The organizer turns on Record and transcribe automatically in the meeting options for each meeting. It's off by default. See Microsoft's page on automatic recording
(opens in new tab)
.

children.q: Does my audio go to the cloud when I record on my own computer?
children.a: Not with Meetily's default setup. The audio is recorded and transcribed on your computer. For summaries, you choose a local model or your own API key. If you use your own key, the transcript text goes to that AI provider to be summarized.

children.q: Does Meetily work with Teams in a web browser?
children.a: Yes. Meetily records your computer's system audio, not just one app. So it captures a Teams call in Chrome or Edge the same way it captures the desktop app.

children.q: Can I use Meetily for an in-person meeting?
children.a: Yes. Start a recording, and Meetily uses your microphone to capture the room. For more tips, see our guide to recording a meeting.

If you own the recording or can edit it, open it and use Video settings → Generate to make a transcript in Microsoft's player. See Microsoft's page on video transcripts

Frequently Asked Questions
What is a second brain for meeting notes?

A second brain is a personal system for keeping what you learn outside your head, so you can find it when you need it.

For meeting notes, it means keeping conversations, decisions, and action items in one place, linked to the right client or project. You can look back at what was discussed, what was agreed, and who needs to do what.

How do I build a second brain like this with Meetily?

You can connect Meetily to Obsidian and an action-item tracker with a small script. Here’s how it works:

Meetily records the meeting and transcribes it on your own Windows or Mac computer. No bot joins the call.
When the summary is ready, Meetily sends your script a signed webhook, an automatic notice that carries the meeting ID but not the notes.
The script gets the meeting title, summary, and timestamped transcript from the local Meetily API. For a quick one-off, the meetily-pro CLI does the same in one command: meetily-pro meetings export <meeting-id> --format md.
An AI model of your choice, either a local model or a provider you pick with your own API key, turns the export into a structured note and a list of action items.
The script saves the note in your Obsidian vault and adds the action items to your tracker, each with an owner and a deadline.

Meetily must be running for this to work. The Meetily API is off by default, so turn it on and set up your own script.

The Obsidian recipe walks you through the setup. The Meetily API docs
(opens in new tab)
 have the full reference, the Meetily CLI guide covers quick commands, and the meetily-workflows GitHub repository
(opens in new tab)
 has example scripts.

Does Meetily work with Obsidian?

Yes. Meetily exports meeting notes as Markdown files that you save straight into your Obsidian vault, with no plugin needed.

A webhook tells your script when a summary is ready, and the script gets the note from the local Meetily API
(opens in new tab)
 (or the meetily-pro CLI), so each note lands in your vault without copying and pasting. Meetily must be running, and your own script handles saving the file.

Follow the Obsidian recipe for the setup instructions.

Can I track action items from meeting transcripts automatically?

Yes. Meetily’s summaries include action items, and your script can fetch them from the local Meetily API
(opens in new tab)
 as JSON, a structured format that’s easy for scripts to work with.

The script can then add those items to your own database or task tracker, with an owner and a deadline for each one. You can then use a dashboard to see what’s overdue, what’s due this week, and what’s slipping.

Is it safe to use AI note takers for confidential meetings?

It depends on where the recording, transcript, and summary go. Check that against your company's confidentiality policy and any client agreements, such as NDAs. Meetily records and transcribes on your own computer by default, and no bot joins the call.

Summaries made with a local model stay on your machine. If you use an AI provider with your own API key instead, the transcript text goes to that provider. See how each AI provider handles your data.

The Meetily API is off until you turn it on. By default it only listens on your own computer, and webhooks carry a meeting ID, not the notes.

Can Meetily summarize a meeting without an internet connection?

Yes. Once you’ve downloaded a local AI model, Meetily can generate meeting summaries on your own computer without an internet connection.

If you use an AI provider with your own API key instead, only the transcript text is sent to that provider.

See how to choose a summary model for more details.

Can I ask Claude or Cursor about my past meetings?

Yes. The Meetily MCP server, built on the same Meetily API, lets AI assistants connect to your meeting data.

You can connect Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or Windsurf, choose what each one is allowed to do, and ask questions like “What did we decide last week?”

Most assistants send what they read to their own AI provider, so only connect the ones you already trust with your meeting notes.

The Decision Maker's Second Brain

How a consultant managing 25 client projects built a private second brain in Obsidian using Meetily transcripts, local AI, and his own automation.

Sandeep Zachariah
CEO, Zackriya Solutions
SEPTEMBER 28, 2026
·
5 MIN READ
·
BUILD IN PUBLIC
·
ENGLISH

TL;DR

A consultant managing 25 major client projects built a private second brain using Meetily. He records and transcribes every client meeting on his own computer, turns each transcript into a structured note in an Obsidian knowledge graph, and tracks action items with owners and deadlines.

Why Meetily: His meetings carry company confidential information. No bot joins the call, transcripts stay on his device, and he chooses which AI processes them.
Two ways to use it: Start with local AI summaries that work without an internet connection. Or send Meetily's output to a folder your other tools can read, and build a workflow around your needs.
What's new: Meetily 1.11.0 adds Meetily Workflows: the local Meetily API, plus webhooks for automation, a command-line tool (CLI) for quick tasks, and the Meetily MCP server for AI assistants. A workflow can now start as soon as a summary is ready, which can replace a daily import script like the one the consultant wrote.

I was on a call with a consultant who manages 25 simultaneous projects. Not small ones: large-scale transformations, enterprise RFPs, multi-country implementations at a company with twelve billion dollars in annual revenue. His commercial team is 250 people. His job is to hold the thread across all of it.

He opened by telling me about a system he'd built. Not a productivity hack.

A system, engineered, layered, deliberate, that does for his memory what no single tool had ever managed to do.

He calls it his second brain.

Every client meeting he records with Meetily. The raw transcript lands on his device. From there, an automation he built picks it up, feeds it through a local AI environment, and converts it into a structured note, the kind of entry he'd want to read before walking into the next meeting with that client. That note goes into Obsidian
(opens in new tab)
, where he's built a knowledge graph
(opens in new tab)
: one node per client, one per project, linked by context, decisions, commitments, open threads.

He also maintains a database of action items pulled from those transcripts (not just his own, but items he's cascaded to his team), each with a deadline and an owner. A personal dashboard sits on top of it, showing him what's overdue, what's due this week, and what's slipping.

The whole system runs on his device. Nothing touches a cloud server he doesn't control.

I asked him why he'd built it around Meetily rather than one of the more polished, cloud-based AI meeting tools.

"The data doesn't leave the device," he said. "That matters when you're working on client projects under NDAs, when you're in commercial discussions that haven't closed, when what gets said in the room needs to stay in the room."

This is the constraint that most AI tools are not designed around. The people with the most sensitive conversations, the ones who most need to capture and organize what gets said in their meetings, are exactly the people who can't send that data somewhere they don't control. The more important the meeting, the more this matters.

What Meetily gives this consultant is not just transcription. It is the infrastructure layer on which a genuinely private second brain can be built. The transcript is the raw material. What you build on top of it is up to you.

The simplest version is the most accessible: every meeting captured, every transcript available, AI summaries generated locally using an open-source model running on your own machine. No internet connection required. No data in transit. You end every call with a document that tells you what was decided, what was agreed, and what you need to do next.

The more sophisticated version is what this consultant built. You change the folder where Meetily stores its output to a location your other tools can read: your Obsidian vault, a shared team drive, a connected database. From there, you attach whatever AI you trust most: a local model if you want zero external exposure, your own private cloud model if you have one, a large language model running behind your own API endpoint
(opens in new tab)
